utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Sofia Nordengren, who has an LLB from the -- I see the court reporter is waiving his hand in distress and shaking his head. He's not hearing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Shall we rise for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Testing, testing. Okay. We seem to be fine again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Sofia Nordengren, who has an LLB from the University of Hong Kong, is originally from Sweden, and is now doing an advanced masters here in the Netherlands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Last week the Chamber informed the parties that the testimony of Mr. Karadzic should start on the 4th of March, 2014. In so ruling, the Chamber had expected to sit four days that week. Unfortunately, due to unforeseen circumstances the Chamber cannot sit on either the 6th or the 7th March. In order not to delay the proceedings, the Chamber has therefore decided to sit on Monday, the 3rd of March, from 11.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m. with the necessary breaks. The Chamber will then sit regular hours on the 4th and 5th of March before adjourning until Tuesday, the 11th of March, as scheduled. The Chamber trusts that with the notice provided, this revision to the schedule will not cause too much inconvenience to the parties. Are there any matters to raise before we continue with the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Somewhat in connection with that. We have been expecting to have the testimony of an official from the Croatian government today to authenticate certain intercepts that were to be offered by the Defence. Last night I received an e-mail, which I forwarded to your staff, indicating that they were expecting that the testimony would take place in March and they didn't plan -- weren't ready to produce the witness for today. So we can file a motion to order the Croatian government to have him here on the 3rd of March, if that's what the Chamber would like. Alternatively, the Prosecution has agreed that the intercepts that we are intending to offer are authentic. As they have taken that same position with respect to our motion to subpoena Witness KDZ145 and with the pending witness who is here in The Hague to testify, KDZ126. So it would be useful for the parties to know whether or not the Chamber would be satisfied to accept the agreement by the parties as to the authentication of these intercepts or whether it still wishes to call the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one modification to Mr. Robinson's remarks. He's quite correct that with respect to the intercept issues that have arisen up until this point, we have taken the same position we did previously with respect to those intercepts and their authentication and for which, I think Mr. Robinson expressed some appreciation the other day since we did so on -- and simply by looking at the material, looking at the previous information available, looking at our previous positions, and taking a consistent position. With respect, however, to the intercepts coming up, we still reserve our position, we're still looking at the specific intercepts and the information we have about that. I'm not suggesting that there will be a different position, but we were looking at that last -- yesterday, we got this material late and this morning. And I hope to get back to Mr. Robinson on that as soon as possible. So I just simply didn't want to preempt our position on the basis of our previous acquiescence, that may well be the case, but we wanted to run through the same process that we engaged in before -- before staking out a particular position. Other than that, Mr. Robinson's submissions are accurate, and I presume it would be helpful for the parties to know where we stood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you expand on the position, Prosecution's consistent position you referred to? What I heard through the legal officer of the Chamber is that the Prosecution would agree to the authenticity in case it can establish the authenticity based on its evidence collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with -- yes, Mr. President. And with respect to the -- the intercepts that have been tendered up to now, up to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not referring to those intercepts which are the subjects of testimony for the forthcoming witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. And I -- maybe it will be clearer if I simply separate the Croatian intercepts that were the subject of Mr. Robinson's remarks with all of the other tendered intercepts. With respect to that latter category, we -- the Prosecution agrees that authenticity is not an issue. I say that was consistent because my recollection is that when there was an effort to tender similar documents from the same sources early in the Defence case, I think that's the position the Prosecution took, that by that time both parties accepted the authenticity of intercepts coming from that same source. So -- however, I think the Prosecution has reserved, again, with respect to that particular category, has reserved its position on the relevance of particular intercepts in contrast to the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What about the eight intercepts that are -- that is the topic of testimony who is coming tomorrow? Am I correct in terms of number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I mean, intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, 145.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or 126, I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution in an e-mail agreed that for those eight intercepts that they were authentic, so I think he can check his e-mails but I'm confident that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm simply double-checking to make sure that I don't confuse dates and numbers. I try to make the distinction in terms of the broader categories, and particularly in terms of the witness that Mr. Robinson was talking about potentially being here on the 3rd. But I have no doubt if he is making the correspondence between our expressed e-mail and that particular witness that his representation is accurate. And I can confirm that now. We have no objection regarding the authenticity of those eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 9.15 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson and Mr. Tieger, coming back to the issue of authenticity of those intercepts in question, the Chamber is of the view that in the circumstances, in light of the facts that the Chamber has so far admitted a number of intercepts pursuant to the evidence of intercept operators as well as a number of interlocutors and that Prosecution can authenticate those intercepts based upon its evidence collection and that there is a genuine agreement between the parties as to their authenticity, the Chamber has a basis to establish the authenticity of those intercepts. I will leave it to the Defence whether to proceed with the evidence of KDZ126 scheduled tomorrow or to resort to bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. We won't be calling that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there are other matters, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, for the record, if the counsel assisting Mr. Jankovic could introduce himself for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Aleksandar Aleksic, attorney at law, and I have been assigned as counsel for Mr. Jankovic by the Registry at his own request. He requested that I represent him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you, Mr. Aleksic. Yes, Mr. Jankovic, would you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Jankovic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I kindly ask you to be mindful of the way we speak and make a pause between question and answers so that the interpretation may be recorded in the transcript. Can you state your full name, father's name, date and place of birth. But slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Jankovic. My father, Dragoja, and mother, Andja. I was born on the 8th of March, 1950, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Equally briefly, can you give us your educational background and profession.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the mechanic school and then went on to the traffic faculty in Zagreb. I went on to take my masters degree in technical sciences in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for being as brief as that. Can you also tell us something about your career.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I got a job on the 1st of November, 1970, in the -- in an organ of internal affairs. I worked in the Prijedor police station as a policeman until 1975, when I transferred to the traffic police department in Prijedor. I was then sent on for schooling. And having completed my schooling, I got the post of traffic policeman. Thereafter, I was the head of the patrolling sector, then assistant commander of the Prijedor police station in charge of the traffic department. On the 19th of August, 1991, I was appointed by the SRBiH MUP as commander of the Prijedor police station. I stayed in that job until the 20th of September, 1991, when the reserve police force was mobilised. On that date, the Prijedor police station ceased to operate in its active force, and the policemen were assigned to eight substations in the municipality of Prijedor. As of the 20th of September, 1991, I was tasked with logistics for the reserve police stations, so I was dealing with supplies. And my concern was to make sure that these reserve police stations in Prijedor were able to operate. This situation prevailed until March of 1993, when I was appointed chief of the public security station in Prijedor upon the removal of the then-chief, Simo Drljaca. However, because my policies clashed, I was removed from that post and was then assistant chief of the police station in Prijedor. In April of 1994, the Republika Srpska MUP appointed me assistant chief of public security -- of the CSB, security services centre. After the Dayton Agreements were signed, I was appointed the deputy chief CSB. And then in 1997 I was appointed chief of CSB. I stayed in that position up until April of 1998 when I was appointed to the post of inspector in the MUP police administration of Republika Srpska. I stayed in that job until 2001 when I had enough years of service to be retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is my understanding correct: From September 1991 to March 1993 you were the logistics chief in the MUP in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I was referring to the MUP, I was referring to the republican level, but it is true that I was logistics chief -- yes, that's -- that's all right. And that was the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: So that was the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Can you tell us the extent of your knowledge about paramilitaries getting organised and illegally armed in the area covered by your station? What was the course of events in that respect?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have very little knowledge about it. I'm not sure what sort of arming you're referring to, the Muslim forces; I mean, the Bosniak forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Outside of the legal process of arming which the JNA was in charge of when it came to its reserve units in the TO, was there any other arming process going on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in a position to see what the level of quality of the communications equipment and the communication itself was between Prijedor and Banja Luka and Prijedor and Pale during the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that between Prijedor and Pale there was no communication whatsoever. No dispatches could be sent. However, between Prijedor and the Pale CSB, there was communication whenever there was power. When there was no power, when there was no electricity, there was no communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 9, it says "during the war." The question was when the war broke out. In line 12, it was Prijedor and the Banja Luka CSB; not Pale CSB.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter confirms that was the case. Indeed, it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Between Prijedor and Banja Luka CSB. There was no communication with Pale either through telegrams or telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter 5560.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the document and what is it about? Are you familiar with this visit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen this before. I can't see the heading. Can we show the heading, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a telefax sent to the Bircan security services on the 5th of August. And that was after the visit which took place on the 27th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen the document before. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it reads --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous page in English, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [As read] "Due to the enormous and vast territory, a high number of inhabitants, poor communication and telephone lines, the ongoing combat, and other elements impacting the formation of the Centre, the objective possibility needs to be looked into," et cetera. How does this fit with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did already say that we had very poor contacts with the Banja Luka CSB on account of the war and power cuts. We didn't have any contact whatsoever with the Ministry of the Interior. For the most part, the contact went through the CSB Banja Luka inspectors who had the supervisory role in respect of the reserve police stations. And specifically, I'm referring to the ones in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the communication like between Prijedor and the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It went through the Banja Luka CSB. The Prijedor station was in fact a substation of the CSB, as it were, CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did the police treat those of its own police officers who committed criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in the area of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that and the centre that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the SJB, under the Law Governing Internal Affairs, it had its duties including the prosecution of such misdemeanors and offenders. Of course, the SJB was charged with detecting and prosecuting such offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2. In English it's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It reads: [As read] "In discussions held at these meetings, competent employees indicated that in addition to cautioning and constant monitoring to ensure a lawful implementation of assignments, they had also suspended several employees, initiated appropriate procedures against them, and placed under wartime assignment some of them within the army." How does this tally with what you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, any police officer who was suspected of misconduct would be taken before a disciplinary court which could render certain decisions. I'm talking about the active police personnel. When it came to the reserve police force, if they were suspected of misconduct, they would be stripped of their status of the reserve policeman and then referred to the secretariat for national defence who would then probably send them on to military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the individuals who appeared to have carried out the inspection and submitted the report; namely, Sreto Gajic and Tomislav Mirosavic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know Gajic. He was the head of the police department at the level of the CSB. These police departments existed only at the level of the CSB. The Prijedor SJB did not have a police department. The Banja Luka police department was the one which would and which did supervise the conduct of the police personnel in this reporting period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4380, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, when it comes to the police in Prijedor, an unavoidable topic is Mr. Simo Drljaca. We often talk about him. First of all, what was his position at that time? Who was in a position to sign documents on his behalf? What was his attitude towards the commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca was appointed as the chief of the public security station at the proposal of the assembly of Prijedor, and that happened on the 16th of April, 1992. He assumed his duties on the 30th of April, 1992. He was the one who had the exclusive right to sign documents on behalf of the public security station. However, I would like to say that on the order of the Prijedor CSB duty service was introduced and that was carried out by inspectors who were on duty 24/7. Chief Drljaca authorised inspectors to sign documents on his behalf when he was absent from the public security station. Those documents were usually dispatches that were sent to the security services centre. Those people were not authors of those dispatches, they just signed them in order to facilitate the dispatch of dispatch of another document to the CSB, if those documents were urgent and couldn't wait for Mr. Simo Drljaca to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was not recorded who the author of those documents was. Let's try and speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that Chief Simo Drljaca authorised inspectors who were on duty to sign certain dispatches or other written documents that were sent to the CSB. Those inspectors were not the authors of those documents and dispatches. Their role was only to sign them, to facilitate the sending of such documents to the CSB. Likewise, when a document arrived from the Banja Luka CSB, a dispatch or some other document, the inspectors would distribute the act. They would make sure that those who needed to know, be aware of the document, were put in the picture. But it was the exclusive task of the chief of the public security station to sign such documents, but when he wasn't there, the inspectors were authorised to sign documents on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you speak a bit more slowly. Did I understand you properly? Was Mr. Drljaca appointed in mid-April? Was there joint power in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you said that he assumed his duties on the 30th of April. Could you please tell us why it took so much time between the appointment and the moment when he assumed duties?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, there was a take-over of power in the municipality. And before the 30th of April, the public security chief was a candidate of the SDA, Hasan Talundzic. On the 30th of April when the power was taken over, the Serbian Democratic Party installed their candidate pursuant to a previous decision of the assembly which was issued on the 16th of April and Simo Drljaca was thus installed on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to find out about the reasons and circumstances of the take-over of power on the 30th of April? Could you please tell us what you saw, what you heard at that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of April at 1400 hours, a meeting was held at the public security station. It was chaired by Chief Hasan Talundzic, and it was attended by all the employees. At the meeting, there was the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, representatives of the parties that were in power and that had their representatives in the Municipal Assembly. The discussion was about finding a compromise for a joint functioning of the public security station. However, towards the end of the meeting when conclusions had to be made about joint functioning and compromise, from the communications centre of the public security station a dispatch arrived in which Chief Delimustafic ordered to stop the columns of the military, to block the barracks, and to start preparations for combat actions in the entire area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That dispatch -- or, rather that dispatch was a consequence of a similar dispatch which was sent by Colonel Efendic, the commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those people who attended the meeting saw that as a declaration of war against the Serbian people and that was also the motive for the take-over of power in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us about Mr. Drljaca? How did he treat crimes and what was his attitude towards co-operation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca, before he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you understand the question, is it? What did you mean, Mr. Karadzic, when you asked how Mr. Drljaca treated crimes? Is it not too general? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency. I'll try and be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Drljaca order people to commit crimes? Did he himself commit crimes or did he try to cover up crimes comitted against anybody; and particularly, Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he never ordered crimes to be committed. He never committed crimes himself. I believe that a large number of the public security station employees were very professional in their work and that they would have never been involved in carrying out an order by any chief which ordered them to commit a crime. And it was their duty to -- not to carry out an order of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he order people to cover up the commission of crimes and to conceal their perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he never ordered any such thing. Or at least I don't know about that. All the crimes that were committed in the territory of Prijedor were processed. An on-site investigation was carried out by the PS Prijedor or if the crime was under the authority of a higher court, then inspectors from the CSB would arrive and carry out an on-site investigation because they were in charge of detecting such crimes and investigating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about subordination? Who was he subordinated to and how did he co-operate with people?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Chief Drljaca was subordinated to the CSB, i.e., to the chief of the CSB in Banja Luka and the minister. He was arrogant. That was his attitude. Sometimes he found himself in situations when he didn't carry out orders, when he objected to orders that he received from the CSB Banja Luka. However, ultimately he was coerced by his superiors to carry out orders and to obey the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn anything about war activities, when they started and how they started in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: After the take-over of power, and we're talking about war activities, ethnically based parties in Prijedor tried to reach an agreement in order to find a solution to the situation that arose after the take-over of power. The situation persisted as sometime after 22nd May, 1992. And then in the village of Hambarine there was an attack on a group of military conscripts who were moving in the direction of Ljubija. That happened in the village of Hambarine. They were attacked by Muslim forces and three military conscripts were killed and two were wounded. After that, on the 24th of April -- or rather, 24th of May, 1992, on the main road leading from Prijedor to Banja Luka in a village called Jakupovici, a military column was stopped -- or rather, it was attacked. There were also casualties on that occasion. They were all military conscripts or army members. On the 30th of May, 1992, there was an attack on the building of the municipality of Prijedor by Muslim paramilitaries. I believe about 500 members of paramilitary units participated in that attack. There was a skirmish between the military and the police of Republika Srpska on the one side and those paramilitaries on the other. There were a lot of casualties on both sides, both killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know and can you tell us about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- the sanitisation operations. After that, who was authorised to do that and what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because you moved away from the topic, it's about Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Jankovic. You said earlier on that Mr. Drljaca never committed crimes himself nor ordered crimes to be committed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then my question for you is this: Did he do everything in order to prevent crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the public security station chief. He reported to both the CSB and crimes services. I know that he never ordered anybody to commit crimes. The police and the crime prevention services worked on the detection and prevention of crimes. He himself never told them not to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 21, it says -- and the witness said he was superior to the public security station and the crime prevention services. He was their boss. That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was their boss. He was the chief of the police and the crime prevention services in the Prijedor public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with so many killed? Who buried the bodies and where? Did the police bury their own? Who buried those who were killed on the side of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the side of the Green Berets, there were the Civilian Protection and the military. I don't know where they buried them. I heard on TV that they were buried in Tomasica, but previously I didn't know where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened next, according to what you knew? What happened with the enemy, with the opponents of the military and the police? Was anybody imprisoned, captured? Did anybody run away? What happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the combat in Prijedor which lasted for nearly the whole year - to be more precise, until the end of that summer, until the end of August - a lot of those members were captured, and especially on the 31st during the attack. When they were captured, members of the Green Berets, they were detained in the Keraterm and Omarska collection centres. They were investigated because they had been involved in the attack. And those who were found to be guilty of the attack on the municipality of Prijedor, measures were taken against them; and those who were not found guilty were released and allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why were the detainees put in Omarska and Keraterm? Did the public security station have its own prison?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the public security station didn't have a prison. They could keep only five, six, up to ten people. However, we are talking about a large number of people, and the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor found Keraterm and Omarska as the most suitable places for those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did the public security station in Prijedor expect to have so many detainees? Was it expecting a conflict? And in your view, how come the conflict in Prijedor started seven weeks after the conflict in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the dispatch sent by Delimustafic and the information that came through the State Security Service, there was an awareness that an attack by Green Berets and the Patriotic League might occur in Prijedor municipality. However, nobody expected the attack to be so fierce, so brutal, or the clash between the Serbian forces and the Green Berets to last for several weeks. However, I didn't understand what you said about Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please refrain from asking a compound question. You are asking so many topics at a time. One at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the conflict, the war began in Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in the beginning of April in Sarajevo, in Brod, and in Kupres, and all these actions indicated that the situation might escalate in our municipality too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come the peace in Prijedor was kept for seven weeks after the war broke out in many places in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor there were constant negotiations and talks and efforts to avoid the war and to resolve the national issue peacefully. However, it turned out later that these talks between the Serbian side and the Muslim side were just taken advantage of by the Muslims to gain time to prepare for the attack. They never had the intention to resolve things peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this case -- or rather, in a different case before this Tribunal, there is an adjudicated fact relating to your role in Omarska; that is adjudicated fact 1130. And I will read it out now in English: [In English] "Dusan Jankovic, commander of the Prijedor police station, supervised the implementation of Simo Drljaca's order of 31st of May, 1992. Dusan Jankovic's duties in this regard were to be carried out in collaboration with the Banja Luka security service centre. His work required the approval of the regional superiors of each branch involved in the operation of the camp." [Interpretation] Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a wrongly adjudicated fact. The truth is that the chief of the public security station drafted an order that was not in accordance with the regulations of internal affairs agencies or in accordance with any law. Under this order, the chief of the public security station in Prijedor places himself above the state security and orders both the state security and the army, which he had no right to do. Second, in this instance the chief of the public security station says that in Omarska the security of the collection centre would be provided by the police station in Omarska. There was no police station in Omarska. There was a reserve police station which had its own commander, assistant commander, and other personnel. Also, in this order the chief of the public security station orders the administration of the mine, which he had no right to do. Everybody knows that the administration of the mine could only receive orders from the Crisis Staff or somebody else higher up in Republika Srpska. This order was never really put into practice, and I had no obligations under this order because as the order itself says, every day the chief of the public security station was briefed by leaders of the groups that conducted interrogation of the detained members of Muslim forces in Omarska. I have never been to Omarska personally, nor did I do anything in connection with that order. And as I said, that order was not really put into practice with the proviso that the security personnel who conducted interrogations briefed the chief of public security stations, Simo Drljaca, every day at a given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was anybody duty-bound to inform you and did you receive any reports about the operation of Omarska or possible violations or crimes committed there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I received no reports whatsoever. The people who worked there reported directly to the chief of the public security station --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Simo Drljaca, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, the passage read out to you as adjudicated fact, you testified they were wrongly adjudicated. But one of the sentence reads like this: "Dusan Jankovic, commander of the Prijedor police station, supervised the implementation of Simo Drljaca's order of 31st of May, 1992." Is it wrong as well? Do you remember what that order was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the content of the order, that fact was adjudicated based on the order as it was written. And in my testimony, I've said that that order was never really put into practice, and I had no need to do anything written in that order because the representatives of the state security, the public security, and the army reported to Simo Drljaca every day on the situation on the ground in Omarska and everything that was going on there and they gave him progress reports. I've also said that Simo Drljaca, with this order, placed himself above the army, the state security, and the administration of the mine which he had no right to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue. But the Chamber needs to rise now before 10.30. Is it a convenient moment, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency. We can and then we can start again whenever you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen to 11.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will break for half an hour and resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let's wrap up the Drljaca topic. Do you know if there was any relationship between me and Drljaca and who would Drljaca be likely to listen to or obey?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: From what I know, he had no contact with you. He was in contact with the Crisis Staff in the territory of Prijedor municipality and with the CSB, the security services centre, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear that the public security station in Prijedor kept the centre in Banja Luka or Pale informed about events in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is also an adjudicated fact -- but first let me see if I understood you correctly. You said that in September 1991 something had happened with police stations -- or rather, the public security station. Can you repeat this. What exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina on 19 September, 1991, issued a decision at its 33rd Session to the effect that the reserve police force should be mobilised in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 20th of September, 1991, the minister of the interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Delimustafic, issued his own order to mobilise the reserve police force in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to the plan that prevailed then, at the police station in Prijedor eight reserve police units were formed. The active duty police station in Prijedor that was active all the way until 20th September, 1991, was disbanded and the personnel was assigned to reserve police stations all over Prijedor. There were eight such reserve police stations and there was the ninth for traffic control. So from that date until the signing of the Dayton Accords, the reserve police stations and the reserve police force remain in place, and each of these reserve police stations had its own commander, deputy commander, and assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to read to you the adjudicated fact 1131 [as interpreted] in English: [In English] "Simo Drljaca was the head of the SJB in Prijedor during the duration of Omarska camp's existence. The uniformed police department of this station was headed by Dusan Jankovic, who was immediately subordinated to Simo Drljaca." [Interpretation] Was there a unified command of the uniformed police after September 1991 and until the Dayton Accords? Is this adjudicated fact 1132 correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. I tried to prove that with a lot of evidence and witnesses, but for reasons unknown to me the Trial Chamber chose to believe the Prosecution who alleged that there was a police station in Prijedor in wartime conditions. It did not exist except on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was able to start operating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure which part is challenged, which is correct and which is not correct. So one of the sentence says: "Drljaca was the head of the SJB ..." Is it correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the second sentence is that the uniformed police department of this SJB was headed by you. Is it correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And is it correct that you were immediately subordinated to Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the employees of the public security station were subordinated to Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that you were immediately subordinated to Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To Drljaca, the chief of the security services centre, and to the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you say it is incorrect to say you headed the uniformed police department of the Prijedor SJB. Then explain why is it incorrect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said here that I was a commander of the peacetime police station in Prijedor. When the reserve police force was mobilised, reserve police stations were also mobilised. And in Prijedor, there were eight of them plus the ninth for traffic control. On the date of mobilisation, 20th September, 1991, the personnel of the peacetime police station were reassigned to various reserve police stations according to their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I continue? Which means that the police station of Prijedor did not begin operating again until the signing of the Dayton Accords and the reserve force of the police was disbanded. I'm trying to emphasise that the peacetime police station did not operate during the war. Its employees were reassigned to reserve police stations and every reserve police station had its own commander, assistant commander, and deputy commander. The deputy commander, assistant commanders, and commanders of reserve police stations were answerable to Simo Drljaca. At Omarska there was a reserve police station of Omarska and they provided the security to the collection centre of Omarska. It was their area of responsibility. I said that I was engage in logistical affairs and I had no responsibility or authority to issue orders to the reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In whose area of responsibility from among these eight territorial stations lay Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Keraterm was in the area of responsibility of the reserve police station number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any powers or any dealings in respect of that station?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it had its own commander, deputy commander, and assistant commander. I didn't have any role to play save for the logistical part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear of any unusual event in the Keraterm station, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that there was a mutiny on the part of the detainees there and that in the process the mutineers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- did you ever hear that the Prijedor police station ever informed the CSB or the ministry at Pale of it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that it informed anybody about it. It could have informed the Banja Luka CSB about it and -- well, that would be my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the detention unit in the public security station was small.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, I'm sorry, the previous adjudicated fact was 1132, not 1131.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the issue of Keraterm and all the events related to it, do you know was Banja Luka or Pale ever informed about it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. It was beyond my line of duty at the time. It may have come from the chief of the public security station, but I don't know and can't speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will read out the adjudicated fact which has to do with the detention cell in the public security station.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's the adjudicated fact 1109.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats were detained at the Prijedor SUP including women and an underage boy." [Interpretation] Were women and minors detained at the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If among those who surrendered on the 30th, there would have been women and children, where would they have ended up? Would they have ended up in detention?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a reception centre or collection centre at Trnopolje where everyone was held, including the able-bodied men, women, children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also on the issue of the detention cell, I will read out the adjudicated fact 1110: [In English] "Detainees at the Prijedor SUP were beaten with metal --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's be clear. You said there was never a woman or minors at Prijedor SUP. Does it mean there was none or you don't know -- you didn't know at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know for a fact that women and children were not taken into custody at the Prijedor SUP. They could only have come to the station asking for help, but there was no case of them being detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we are with this issue, were Muslim civilians confident enough to come to the station? Did they feel safe enough?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. All the citizens were free to come to the police station that was active in their neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now read out the adjudicated fact 1110.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Detainees at the Prijedor SUP were beaten with metal objects by members of the intervention squad including Dado Mrdja. The detainees were beaten during interrogation and humiliated. The detainees were subjected to ethnic slurs." [Interpretation] Did this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure it was correctly translated. First sentence should read: "Detainees at the Prijedor SUP were beaten ..." Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That's how I read it out but I see it wasn't recorded. Detainees at the Prijedor SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, there were no detainees at the Prijedor SUP. It was a holding cell. And a very small one. I said that people who were under investigation or interrogation were at Keraterm and Omarska. The others who were seeking a safe place to stay or refuge were at the Trnopolje reception centre. When somebody was taken in for an interview or some other processing, perhaps, but I am not aware of there having been beatings from any side. I don't know what this adjudicated fact is based on. To the best of my knowledge, this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The adjudicated fact 1113 reads: [In English] "Prior to their transfer, the detainees were forced to run a gauntlet of policemen." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no gauntlet of policemen there. As far as I know, that's how it was. I have no other knowledge that would disprove this, what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Adjudicated fact 1281 -- 82. 1282 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean by saying: "I have no other knowledge that would disprove this"? So it sounds as if you do not exclude there might have been such a gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am claiming that there was no gauntlet whatsoever. It could not have happened at the public police station. Now, if somebody hit somebody else, I cannot possibly know about this. But had there been knowledge of such a police officer behaving this way, there would most certainly have been some sort of a response or repercussions coming from the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In lines 6 and 7 it should read that: "If there had been such cases, then they would have been isolated outbursts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say: "I cannot possibly know about this"? I will read out the sentence: "Now, if somebody hit somebody else, I cannot possibly know about this." You said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Adjudicated fact 1282 reads: [In English] "In May 1992, the Carsijska mosque was destroyed. A group of men, including a body-guard of Simo Drljaca, Milorad Vokic, set the main mosque in Prijedor alight." [Interpretation] Is this adjudicated fact correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Vokic did not exist. This name is not among those listed in the public security station. There was Radovan Vokic. He was Simo Drljaca's driver. And given that I know the man, he could not have possibly done something of this sort. He was a professional and would never do anything like this. I'm speaking from my knowledge of him. Perhaps if he was mentally deranged he would have done something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there cases where religious facilities were torched and how did the authorities treat such cases?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what the attitude of the members of the Prijedor SJB was in respect of incidents such as this one. Any incidents which would happen in the area within the purview of the SJB would be followed up by a team of police officers attending the scene. In some of these cases, which I didn't see for myself, I know that this is how it was done and this is how the Law on Internal Affairs envisaged it: Members of the crime service would attend the scene, examine the scene, and then file a criminal report against the unidentified perpetrator. The activities that would follow would be ones to detect or identify the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you agree that the Carsijska mosque was destroyed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you also agree it was set alight by a group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in what way it was done, but I know that this bulb was used --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That this mosque was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 13 it wasn't interpreted when the witness said that there were such cases. And then the rest is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say at the start of your answer that there were such cases?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D49102.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have a translation yet, but I'll kindly ask you to speak slowly and introduce the document to us. The 28th of August, 1992. Can you tell us what this is, who issues the document, and what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is about the basic court in Prijedor, record of on-site investigation, compiled on the 29th of August, 1992, by the duty investigating judge of the basic court in Prijedor, as a follow-up to the destruction of religious buildings; namely, the Catholic church and mosque, where two people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: So this is a record made as a result of an on-site investigation into the destruction of a Catholic church and mosque which was compiled on the 29th of August, 1992, by the basic court in Prijedor or its investigating judge. And as I said, an on-site investigation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is stated that Dragosavljevic, Zivko, the duty investigating judge, conducted the on-site investigation along with crime inspectors; Rade Knezevic, a forensic officer; et cetera. And it reads below that the on-site investigation team found at the scene the physician, Dr. Ivic, and a lieutenant from the military security. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know the doctor and this is the first time I see that a physician was found at the scene where an on-site investigation was conducted. So this is a report compiled by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top it says that the locals were interviewed, that Milan Prastalo, an explosives expert, examined the scene. And further down, it reads, the third paragraph from the top, that: Many residential and office buildings in the immediate vicinity were damaged. What does this high extent of damage indicate to your mind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: All these were observations made by the on-site investigation team. As for the destructive force of the explosion, it indicates that those who were behind the explosion were not professional. This was not done professionally. Had it been done so, there would not have been such a high degree of damage inflicted to the surrounding buildings. In a word, it was a group that wasn't apt in handling explosives that were used to commit this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when it comes to Tombor, Slobodan [phoen], who was a member of the military security organs, why was he involved? Why do you think?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the military security sent their own man because it was the area of responsibility of the 43rd Brigade in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the mine, were there any explosives there? Did the army have explosives? What could have been the origin of the explosives that were used?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the mine did have explosives, that the army also had them, the public security station didn't have explosives, nor did it ever handle explosive devices. When explosive devices were detected, then they reported such cases and then professionals were sent. Sappers were sent to the site to remove those explosives. I don't know the origin of the explosives in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D4381, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D49406. Perhaps it's 106. I apologise. 1D49106.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, just briefly, could you just tell us about the nature of this document, again in light of the previous document, that previous document was issued by the Court. And what this is this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a record of an on-site investigation compiled by the SJB, i.e., the on-site investigation team which was involved in the investigation on the 29th of October, 1992. After a fire had broken out during the night between the 28th of October and 29th of October and when the mosque in Gornja Puharska near Prijedor was involved in that fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it says here that the on-site investigation was attended by Mrs. Dusanica Gavranovic, who was the person in charge of the -- of the shop nearby. In what cases were citizens requested to attend on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why she was called. Maybe she was a witness, maybe she knew something, which is why the investigation team wanted to talk to her in order to obtain evidence as to who might have been the perpetrator of the act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who were usually perpetrators of such crimes according to what you know and what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Some renegades who were neither members of the army nor the police, but they thought that they had the right to commit such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This on-site investigation was carried out by the public security station of Prijedor. What happened next? When such a document was issued, what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: When a document of this kind was issued, it was forwarded to the investigating judge, accompanied by all the necessary documents, and then it was forwarded to the public prosecutor's office, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and also marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D4382, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could the witness please be shown 1D49103.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We had a document issued by the court, another by the police station, and this one was issued by the prosecutor's office in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was issued by the prosecutor's office. The document was issued on the 14th September, 1993. It was sent to the chief of the public security station in Prijedor, requesting the necessary documents to be sent to them, meaning all the evidence collected in the pre-trial procedure. This is consistent what I said about the judge and the prosecutors office. Mr. Knezevic was the person who collected the evidence and he personally is hereby requested to submit all the data to the public prosecutors office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So is this in connection with the document that we showed you first about the destruction of the mosque? And now we can see that the prosecutor is already in touch with the police requesting that the police undertake further activities with this regard?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for the identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4383, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 1D149101 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D49101. This is the document. It's not very legible but maybe you will be able to help us with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this? This is a criminal report; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a criminal report which was issued in 1993. It was signed by Bogdan Delic, who was chief at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what were the crimes? Damage to the road is subject; right? The mosque?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not very legible, but I can see it is about the mosque which was destroyed and there were casualties. A married couple was killed. It's a criminal report which was sent to the prosecutor's office in Prijedor. And it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no objection to it being MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D4384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the Catholic church in Surkovac, did you hear about that? What happened to that church? What was done thereafter according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the church was damaged. I know from people's stories. There were talks about that in the public security station. I don't know what happened thereafter. I suppose that there was an on-site investigation. In the position that I occupied, I was not aware of all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've got the document on the screen. The number is 1D49105.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what the document is.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is information about the destruction of the Roman Catholic church in Surkovac. I don't see who the author of the document was. In any case, the Roman Catholic church in Surkovac fell within the zone of responsibility of the public security station in Ljubija, which was about 20 kilometres from the town of Prijedor itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the penultimate paragraph it says that from interviews with the villagers and the parish priest, we could not learn anything about the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please scroll up a little? Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that no information was obtained about possible perpetrators, what happened next? Here an investigating judge is mentioned. His name was Trivan Jovicic. Do you know Mr. Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the investigating judge of the basic court in Prijedor, and he was together with the authored officials of the public security station. When the on-site investigation was carried out, the complete documents were compiled, and certain conclusions can be drawn from the documents about the explosion and its consequences, which means that there will be further actions in order to detect the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the same Trivan Jovicic, who is the liaison officer with the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's the one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last document in this series is 1D49104.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you help us with this? The basic court in Prijedor made its own record on the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Trivan Jovicic. It's not very legible, so I can't see which members of the crime service of the public security station in Prijedor were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the same incident in Surkovac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this is a record of the on-site investigation in Surkovac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph it says the place of the incident was photographed and a sketch was made. And the photos and the sketch are an integral part of the record.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That was part of the customary procedure. An on-site investigation was carried out, the record of the investigation was signed by Jovan -- Trivan Jovicic, who was the investigating judge in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4386, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, can you tell us, please, in addition to the places where there was combat and casualties on both sides, were there villages in Prijedor, and I mean Muslim and Croatian villages, which did not engage in fighting and which did not suffer any consequences or damage?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There was Muslim villages like Gornja and Donja Puharska, Rakovac, Gomjenica, Tukovi, Zecovi, Donja Ljubija, and some other villages. I know that there were no war activities in those villages. The Patriotic League or the Green Berets were not organised in those villages. Wherever the Green Berets or the Patriotic League were organised and where there were preparations for war, there were skirmishes between the Serbian army and Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the village of Cerici? What was the majority population there? Was there any combat going there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a Muslim village. Brezicani, the same, no combat there. Donja and Gornja Puharska. Over 95 per cent of the villages were Muslims. No fighting ever happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the village of Cela? What was the majority population there? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many but there were a majority Muslim population. There no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Gornji Volari and Ravska? What was the majority population? Was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The majority population were Croats. There was no fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to talk about the crimes which happened in Koricanske Stijene. Can you briefly tell us about that crime? How was it portrayed in the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in your case? In very short outlines, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was charged with that crime before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although I didn't know that that convoy had been planned. However, before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were two types of witnesses; or, rather, two categories of witnesses. One category of the witnesses were those who were escorting the convoy. I don't know whether they also participated in the crime itself. They were never processed and the prosecutor tasked them with providing false evidence in order for the others to be charged with the crime and convicted of it. The other category of the witnesses were those who had been processed, who had participated in that crime, who plea bargained with the prosecutor in order to have their sentences reduced. However, their task was to provide false testimony before the trial chamber. I would like to say here that I had worked in the police for 30 years. I was not familiar with any case like I witnessed in front of the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the prosecutor had a list of witnesses -- a list of questions that they gave to the witnesses to learn by heart and to testify by those who needed to be convicted. I believe that in the proceedings before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when it came to Koricanske Stijene, those who really perpetrated that crime were not convicted of the crime. They still walk freely through the streets of Prijedor and some other towns. Those who were found guilty were those that false witnesses accused on the instructions of the prosecutor. Here it is considered an adjudicated fact that I was up there. It says in my final decision: "He did not commit crime. It was not proven that he issued any orders. He was there." So the fact was established based on what the false witnesses said, that I was there, and that's why I was convicted. However, there were legally remedies, and I believe that if justice needs to be satisfied when it comes to Koricanske Stijene, there will have to be a retrial in order to establish who the perpetrators were and to bring those people to justice, not only because of me who was falsely accused and unjustly convicted but also because of all the people who had been killed there. To try and to convict innocent people for what had happened up there is no -- is not comforting for the families of the victims of that crime. So this is what I have to say in response to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That was 21 August, 1992. I was on duty at the police station from 0700 hours until the 21st at 0000 hours. There is a lot of evidence and a lot of witnesses that I called to prove this. After 0700 hours on the 21st, I took the service car, Volkswagon Golf, went home, had breakfast, had coffee, took some cheese, and went to Bosanska Dubica, which is now called Kozarska Dubica municipality, a place called Sereflije [phoen], to a celebration, a family celebration. I called a number of witnesses to prove this and wanted to call as many more but the trial chamber refused to hear them. After that in the evening I brought back the service car to the police station and went home. That is the truth, but unfortunately the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not accept it. We will continue trying to prove the real truth and that is my purpose, to come to the real truth and prove it in the case of Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the police in that convoy and in similar convoys? Did they organise it and what was their task?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could they, both, please, observe a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please put a pause between the question and answers. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not the police, the milicija, that organised the convoy. The convoy was organised by the Crisis Staff and the Red Cross of Prijedor municipality; the latter, headed by Srdo Srdic, deputy.
