The public security station's task, at the request of the Crisis Staff and the Red Cross, was to provide an escort to this convoy. And it was mainly members of the intervention platoon who were on this escort detail. The intervention platoon was established for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before and after the 21st of August, were there other similar convoys travelling to Croatia or to central or western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before that there were convoys, I don't know how many, and after the 21st of August, 1992, there were other convoys travelling to Croatia. I think, in fact, after that date there was one convoy that went from the collection centre of Trnopolje some time in September or October the same year, and that one travelled to Croatia, Bosanski Novi, Dvor na Uni, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before or after, did anything similar happen that could help predict this event, this incident?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no such thing before or after. That was the only time when such a crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Jankovic, earlier on, it's transcript page, end of page 45, you said that: "Those who really perpetrated that crime were not convicted of the crime. They still walk freely through the streets of Prijedor and some other towns." So it sounds as if you knew who perpetrated that crime. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no proof for my assertion, but I want to say the following: As far as the perpetrator or perpetrators of this crime are concerned, we should look for them among the protected witnesses who have never been prosecuted, people who escorted this convoy, because it's not possible for people who were not there to be guilty, whereas those who actually escorted the convoy are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- walking free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Simply my question is: Do you know or do you not know the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know and I have no proof, but I have my assumptions. I have my ideas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 10, your Excellency -- his Excellency, Judge Kwon, asked "it sounds as if you knew," and now it's been misinterpreted again. Not "as if you know" but "as if you knew" was the question. Tell me, did you know something at that time? And if not at that time, then when did you exactly learn something that made you suspect?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about the event on the next day, on the 21st of August from the head of the public sector of the police station, Mr. Bulic. When I came on the 22nd to the public security station, the secretary of the commander of the reserve police station, Milutin Cadjo, told me that somebody called from Banja Luka, from the CSB, and said that Milutin Cadjo and I should report to Banja Luka, to the chief. When we came to his office, he was not there. We waited for 15, 20 minutes, and then he showed up. He said he was at a meeting with the chief, Djuro Bulic, and that Simo Drljaca had been there too, and he showed us a dispatch from the commander of the 22nd Light Brigade, Colonel Peulic, and he read out that dispatch to us. And when he finished reading, Cadjo and I were astounded that something like that could have happened. And all the three of us were very hard hit by that crime, especially because the assumption was the police had committed it; more precisely, the intervention platoon. That is how I found out that a crime had been committed. Then followed the investigation, and I don't know how far it went, but I know there was an inquiry into the Koricanske Stijene incident, both by the security services centre and the investigating judge and the public prosecutor in Banja Luka. I believe members of the army were also involved in the investigation or inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us what happened with the perpetrators after that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've said here that I have my ideas about who could have committed this crime, but I have no certainty. I can only suppose. There were proposals that people from the escort detail be arrested and prosecuted. However, the members of the intervention platoon who were on the escort detail, along with other members who were not on the escort detail, escaped to Kozara when they realised they could be arrested. They resisted arrest and then followed negotiations with the chief of the public security station. But the chief of the public security station was not able to carry out the order of the CSB Banja Luka, so the intervention platoon was disbanded and placed at the disposal of the army and its members were sent to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How big was that platoon? How big was each of its squads? And tell the Chamber, what is Kozara?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's Mount Kozara, actually, a mountain that stretches above the Prijedor municipality and connects it to Banja Luka on the right-hand side and Bosanski Novi, or, rather, Novi Grad, on the left-hand side. It's Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How large was the intervention platoon? How many squads did it have, what was the number of men, and how many weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The intervention platoon had two squads of reserve police, 20 members each. That's 40 total, plus the commander, which makes it 41. They were armed with infantry weapons. Each squad had a combat vehicle, a so-called BRD, an armoured combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why was Simo Drljaca unable to have them all arrested?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There would have been bloodshed. Later on we listened to him a lot on the subject, and he said a compromise had been made to send them to the front line where it was a big question whether they would survive. And if any came back, then they would be prosecuted. I believe disbanding this unit and sending them to the front line was a compromise, which in the opinion of the chief of the public security station and the chief of the CSB Banja Luka, was the most acceptable solution, because they certainly would have resisted arrest and it could not be done without bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that one squad was on the escort detail and the other squad, which wasn't on the escort detail, also escaped to Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They went to Kozara all together and they wanted to show in that way that they were intent on resisting arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was any action taken to suspend the judicial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I've already said that both the public security station and the public prosecutors office and the high court in Banja Luka and also the military security service were involved in shedding light on this incident. I don't know whether it was suspended or how far it went. I've told you all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that those were reserve policemen, what kind of police training did they have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, to be inducted into the reserve police force one had to be vetted, just like active duty policemen. After that, they went through a preparation course learning about the rules and procedures in internal affairs organs. However, when the war began, as far as this intervention platoon is concerned, there was no vetting and the regular procedure was not observed. Everything was done on the run, so there was no vetting, no education, no training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why was there no vetting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was wartime. There was no time for that. Units such as the intervention platoon recruited men who were fearless, who were willing to go to war, whereas active duty policemen tried to avoid going to the front line and getting involved in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. I have nothing further at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You alluded several times to your own trial. I just want to get some facts straight about that. You were recently tried by the Bosnian state court together with three former members of the Prijedor police intervention platoon for the Koricanske Stijene massacre. And in February of 2013, you were convicted and you are currently serving a sentence of 21 years; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the state court rejected your claim that you repeated several times in your testimony today, that you had no command position in the Prijedor SJB at the time but that you were merely carrying out logistics tasks. The court concluded that you were discharging the function of commander of the Prijedor police station, which it found continued to function during the war, and that you de facto had the status of deputy chief of the Prijedor SJB. That's what the court found; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was found but that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the court also rejected your alibi defence, which you also repeated today, that you were in Bosanska Dubica on the day of the massacre. The court concluded, based on the testimony of multiple eye-witnesses, that you met the convoy at Tukovi on the day of the massacre in an official police vehicle, and you led the convoy dictating its stops and its movements. That's what the court concluded; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what the court concluded. However, they relied on the witnesses that I mentioned a moment ago. There was a number of witnesses, two or three I believe, who said they had seen me when the convoy was leaving Tukovi from the direction of Prijedor. And there was only one witness in the entire proceedings who said he had seen me onboard on vehicle. I challenge the testimony of that witness and I believe that witness had entered into a deal with the prosecution and received a lesser sentence than the sentence the others received. The others received 30 years imprisonment and he got 13. I challenge his testimony, I believe it was a lie, and I will resort to legal remedies in further proceedings to prove that he perjured himself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, line 25, it says: "I believe it was a lie." The witness didn't say he believed. He claimed it was a lie. And also in line 9, we read "it was found," but that's wrong. The correction translation would be "it was a wrongly established fact."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can understand that. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the court -- in respect of your own liability, the court concluded that although after the convoy stopped at the execution site, you continued to escort the remainder of the convoy to its final destination. They held that you must have known about and intended the killing of the separated men given your position and role in the police, your presence at the execution site where the preparations for the massacre were carried out, and the fact that you spoke with members of the intervention platoon at the execution site. That's what the court concluded; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There was not one witness of the prosecution in my trial who said I followed them or escorted them to the execution site. If that was written as a finding, then it's not true. There was this one witness who entered into a deal who said he had seen me, but he said he had seen me onboard a vehicle at the place where some of them were separated. The other witnesses didn't speak of seeing me up there. That's one thing. Second, I was born in Prijedor. I finished high school there. I worked on the police force for 20 years until that date, the 21st. If there were, as the prosecution claims, 1200 Muslims in that convoy, is it possible that not a single Bosniak who had seen me there? They didn't find one single Bosniak who had seen me. They found one person who said that he had seen me in order to get a lesser sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 26029, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It hasn't been released, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you can try again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Jankovic, this is the cover page of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to page 115 of the B/C/S and page 22 of the partial translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 499. And this is where the court discusses the witnesses who testified as to your presence that day in escorting the convoy. And it starts out by saying: "The fact that the accused Jankovic came to Tukovi in a police Golf together with witness K-2, is stressed consistently by Damir Ivankovic, Gordan Djuric, and Ljubisa Cetic ..." And then about halfway down the page -- halfway down the paragraph, and this is on the next page in the B/C/S, the court says: "As K-2 points out, Jankovic and another police officer were in this vehicle," referring to the official Golf vehicle. And the last sentence: "Witness K-A1 also stresses that in Tukovi the accused Jankovic, along with some other active policemen, got into a police Golf." So you've been stressing that it was just one witness that the court relied on, but here in this paragraph you can see there were five or six people who testified as to your presence in the -- at the convoy; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we show him the 499 paragraph, the first part of the 499.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I start? May I read this out?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: First, Mr. Jankovic, do you agree or disagree that the court relied on six witnesses to confirm your presence that day in Tukovi and leading the convoy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Here it goes: I challenge the witness statements and the adjudicated fact. It states here that together with Witness K-2, I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't state the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not. Witness K-2 gave a statement to the members of the SIPA --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: May I? Please, may I just say why I disagree with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Jankovic, but that wasn't my question. I understand that you disagree with it. My question was very simple as to whether or not you agree what -- that the court relied on six witnesses who said they saw you in Tukovi leading the convoy.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: First, I would like to tell you something about K-2. He never said this. Further, Damir Ivankovic did say it, Gordan Djuric never said it, and Ljubisa Cetic did say it. So we're not discussing six witnesses here, we're discussing Damir Ivankovic and Ljubisa Cetic who concluded a plea bargain in order to get lesser sentences. K-2 was part of the escort in the Golf. His statement to the SIPA members was that he, Vladimir Sobot, and Miroslav Paras were in the car. Vladimir Sobot gave the same statement. He was on the escort. It was only Ljubisa Cetic who said that I was on the escort for that stretch of the road. We are discussing the location called Tukovi where the column started its journey. The place where the crime was committed was between 250 and 300 kilometres away from this spot. I don't see any other witnesses here. I can only find Damir Ivankovic and Ljubisa Cetic. The others didn't state that. And the two are witnesses that entered into a plea bargain with the prosecution in order to get more lenient sentences. And they were on the escort of the convoy and they confessed to the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 23 in the English and page 116 in the B/C/S. Paragraph 502 and 503.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, this is where the court drew its conclusions as to your responsibility. And in paragraph 502 the court concludes that given your -- given its finding that you were dictating the tempo of the column's movements and its stops and having in mind your position and role, you had to have been aware of what was going to happen. And in paragraph 503, it refers to its finding that you got out of the -- your vehicle at the execution site, spoke with Paras and Mrdja, and concluded that you must have known, again, about the intent. And at the bottom of the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is on the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- the court says: "However, the very presence of the accused Jankovic there, at the location where all the preparations for the planned massacre that followed were carried out, also his contacts and conversations with persons who are the director perpetrators of that killing."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "And finally, the testimony on the act itself of the separation of the men that took place at the location." The chamber says: "This points to only one conclusion: That this accused was aware and that he wanted the onset of the consequence prohibited by law and shared the intent of those accused of the crime that followed." Now that, in a nutshell, is -- are the court's findings on your criminal responsibility for the executions; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The chamber established this fact on the basis of a single witness statement. The only witness who, besides, entered into a plea bargain and had to say something in exchange for a more lenient sentence, and this is what he said. There were no other witnesses and I said there were over a thousand Muslims. At least one of them should have seen me there and would have been able to confirm my presence there. I challenge this fact and I assert that the statement made by this witness is false.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender the pages that we have referred to in this judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure how it would assist the Chamber. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I thought it had been our practice to simply read out those portions and then have it not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, relevant portions was put to the witness and we heard the evidence. I don't see the need to admit this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 26038, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Jankovic, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Witness said in his answer that, I don't remember the name of the place, but the location of where he made the stop was in dispute in his trial. Do you confirm that, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I don't believe there was -- he -- he denied being a part of the convoy whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said it's 200 kilometres away, but in that paragraph it's in the very proximity from the execution site. Was it one of the issues?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow, Your Honours. The witness denied being any part of the convoy. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I see paragraph 501.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Serbian version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page, 502 probably. In the middle, 502 says: "The location where the last stop was made, which is a location in the immediate proximity of the execution site ..." And shall we go back to 501. Yes. I see in 499 "Tukovi," so are we referring to the same place? Tukovi and the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Tukovi was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- last stop?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Tukovi was where the convoy commenced which is quite some distance from the execution site. That's my understanding. The findings were did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So where did the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The findings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- see Mr. Jankovic? At Tukovi or the last stop?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But not all witnesses. Some witnesses saw him in Tukovi and others saw him at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you Your Honours -- I've finished with this topic if Your Honours wish to take the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not some but one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we take a break? We resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have 65 ter 26038, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Jankovic, you stated in your testimony several times that you did not have the position of commander of the Prijedor police station in 1992. And, in fact, the police station ceased to operate in September of 1991 and that persisted for the duration of the war. And you can see here this document is a list of Prijedor police station staff to receive a salary for the period 16 April to 15 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That is your signature. You signed under the title, "Station Commander"; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You signed this payroll list for April and May 1990 for Prijedor police station staff as Prijedor police station commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have the first page again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a list of the police employees of the SJB Prijedor for the period between 16 April and 15 May 1992. It's a payroll list, which I signed as commander of this police station. However, as I said, when mobilisation took place and the reserve police stations were set up, this station ceased to operate and the police officers who worked here were assigned to the eight reserve police stations as of the 20th of September, 1991. Why was this list drawn up? Well, because members of the active police force who were permanently employed with the MUP, unlike the reserve police force, received their salary differently, from a different source. Here, the Banja Luka CSB chief wanted a list of the police employees in the Prijedor SJB in peacetime. And this is a list of the members of the police who were reassigned to the reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So it is your position that even though this list states that it is a list of Prijedor police station staff to receive a salary and it is signed by you as station commander, that in fact none of these people worked for the Prijedor police station and the station did not exist and you were not the commander. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I wasn't commander of the police station. I was the commander of the Prijedor police station in peacetime between the 19th of August, 1991, and March 1993. The only difference being that I did not command over this police station because its members were reassigned to reserve police stations and the work of this station ceased. It was only reactivated after the demobilisation following the signing of the Dayton Accords, but it did not operate in the period indicated here. It was an organisational unit operational in peacetime within the MUP and within the Banja Luka CSB. However, it stopped working the day mobilisation took place and the day its workers or members were reassigned to police -- reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 26040. And I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, 2603 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't think I understood the witness at all. Could you tell us in a nutshell why you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The request was made for a list of active members of the police to be drawn up for payroll purposes. These were people who were in permanent employment with the MUP; specifically, the Banja Luka CSB. In peacetime, they came under the Prijedor police station. At the time this list was drawn up, this peacetime Prijedor police station was not operational because as of the 20th of September, 1991, its members were reassigned to reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. When did you sign this document? It's sometime May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Why did you sign this document at that time in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because information was requested concerning the members of the Prijedor police station. These people, although they were reassigned to reserve police stations, nevertheless continued receiving their salaries from a different source than those who were reserve police members. You had several categories. You had the category of those unemployed, employed, and retirees. All these different categories received their benefits differently and thus the active police members received their salary differently than the ones who were reserve members. And I said that this list concerned those who, up to -- who from the 20th of September, 1991, up until the Dayton Accords were actually active police members of SJB Prijedor. So this is a list of active members of the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's forget in what capacity they worked at the time, but it's true they worked at the Prijedor police station at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were members of the Prijedor police station in peacetime. At the time when this list was drawn up, they were members of the reserve police stations within the area of Prijedor. And I said that there were eight of these reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did adduce several pieces of evidence before the court in the BiH attesting to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The list of members that you see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can understand so far. But I am not sure I heard your answer why you signed this document as a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because I was asked to produce a list of members of what was in peacetime the Prijedor police station, simply because they were paid differently than were those who were members of the reserve police force. The reserve police force present in these reserve police stations were not staff in permanent employment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were those policemen who were members of the police in peacetime called as uniformed policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were members of the reserve police stations as well, eight of them, between 20 September, 1991, and the signing of the Dayton Accords. Only when the Dayton Accords were signed and the reserve police force was disbanded did this station start to operate again, of course with a different commander, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can you say that you headed the uniformed policemen at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Each reserve police station had its own commander, deputy commander, and assistant commander. They were answerable directly to the SJB chief, Drljaca. This station was not operational at the time. It was dormant because it was active only in peacetime. So I was its commander in peacetime. And that was the state of play [as interpreted] pursuant to decisions that had been taken before the war and concerned this particular police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But still I can't understand then why you signed this as a commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, why did I sign? I just said why. They were asking me to produce a list of the SJB Prijedor members for the purposes of payroll for this particular period, between 16 April and 15 May. I had been commander of the Prijedor police station and therefore I produced this list. But this station itself was not operational within the organisational scheme. Rather, its activities were transferred on to the reserve police stations, and this was the situation that applied not only to Prijedor but to all the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in wartime circumstances. Mobilisation plans were activated and this particular station was disbanded or its members were reassigned to reserve police stations. Similarly, workers in a company which in peacetime had their wartime assignments, these wartime assignments would re-assign them either to the military or the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 15, it says: [In English] "And that was the state of play...," and the witness said "that was the way people were paid before the war," not "the state of play before the war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That seems to be the case. Do you confirm that, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Karadzic's correction is correct. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have 65 ter 26039. And I don't think we got a number yet for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6674, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't need the translation of other parts? Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you can see this is a report from the Prijedor SJB on duties and assignments carried out for April 1992, and it's dated May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, that is your signature. You signed this document as station commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Could I please see the first page or the heading of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the Ministry of the Interior of Sarajevo, CSB Banja Luka, public security station Prijedor, report on duties and assignments carried out in the month of April 1992. That's what I read on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'd like you to recognise your signature on the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That is your signature under the title: "Station Commander, Dusan Jankovic," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This should not have been signed by station commander but the chief, Simo Drljaca. This is not one and the same document. This is my signature and I was the station commander, but this does not refer to the public security station but to the police station. I really don't know. It should have read "police station Prijedor," not the public security station. On the first page, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure what your claim is here. Is it your claim that this document is somehow not authentic or is it your claim that this is a mistake that you signed under the title station commander, Dusan -- wait, wait --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Wait, please, for the question.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is it your claim that this document is not authentic or is it your claim that it is a mistake that you signed this document under the title: "Station Commander, Dusan Jankovic."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I never said that I was not the commander of the peacetime police station. I've repeated that often. There is nothing in dispute there. But this should have been signed by somebody else, not the station commander. I don't understand this. I never saw that the commander of the police station signed the document that belonged to the public security station. The police station is one part of the public security station, one part of its organisational scheme. This is my signature. It hasn't been forged. But I can't say that the document is authentic. This is something that should be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You can see that the first paragraph states the Prijedor police station continued to work on maintaining and improving the favourable law and order situation. And in the fourth paragraph, it says that the station filed a total of six reports. You have emphasised numerous times that the Prijedor police station did not operate during this period of time. This document makes clear that the Prijedor police station was in fact functioning in April 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't function and I claim that. And I dispute your claim. The truth is that the police station existed. It is possible that it filed reports to the CSB. As reports --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you speak very slowly so that we can follow. Could you repeat from where you said: "The truth is that the police station existed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that it exists. The police station existed in peacetime. At that time the police station did not function. It -- only the reserve police stations functioned. This could only be a report -- as a collective report on the work of the police, a collective report on the activities of all the employees of the reserve police stations, and it was sent to the CSB Banja Luka. I never said that the police did not submit reports. I have never disputed that a report went to Banja Luka. What I dispute here the fact that the commander of the police should sign reports by the public security stations, because a public security station is an institution of a hierarchy rank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last sentence of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that this report was sent by the public security station in Prijedor, and it should have been signed by chief of the public security station, not the commander. That's why I don't understand that a report of this kind, issued by the public security station, could have signed by somebody whose title is station commander. I was, indeed, authorised to sign reports and so were 90 inspectors in the public security station, but I was not authorised to sign as the police station commander but as a person who was authorised by the chief of the public security station in Prijedor to sign documents on his behalf when he was absent so that they could be dispatched to the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Forget the first passage, Mr. Jankovic. Please take a look at the first paragraph of this page. Does this refer to Prijedor public security station or Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first paragraph of this page, the first paragraph you are seeing now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this report, which was compiled, there are also activities of the police station, the crime service, the communications services centre. This report follows the organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as it existed in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the first paragraph. Just two lines -- or three lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the first paragraph. All right. And it is true that there are references to the active duty police station in Prijedor, but I'm saying that in addition to the police there are also activities of crime prevention services, the communication services centre, the legal affairs, and all the other organisational units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I. Transcript, translation, interpretation. Transcript line 9, page 70, the witness didn't say "90 inspectors" but "10 inspectors." And as for the first line on this page, where it says: "The activities of the police station in Prijedor has been slated as the Prijedor police station continued to work, and so on and so forth." [In English] I would rather translated: "The activity of police station on the maintenance and improvement of favorable law and order." A little bit different translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So activities of the Prijedor police station continued. Why don't you read the first line in B/C/S so that we can hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When it comes to maintaining and improving the favourable law and order situation on the territory of the municipality in April 1992, continued in April 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think we heard the correct translation. I didn't hear any Prijedor police or something. Could you read again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read slowly. "When it comes to the activities of the police station in Prijedor ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would also translate it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we'll deal with that in a separate course of action. Shall we continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'd tender this document, and I'd like 65 ter 26040, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6675, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you can see this is a document of a very similar format to the previous document, also dated May 1992, but it is the work-plan for the month of May 1992 of the Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, if we could go to the last page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, that is your signature under the title: "Station Commander Dusan Jankovic"; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same mistake --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as in the previous document, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would also like to see the second page to which it refers to. To which organisation does this first paragraph refer to, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The public order situation in the precinct of the Prijedor police station is as favorable as in March 1992, which can be seen from the fact that 6 misdemeanor reports were filed against 9 individuals for 8 offences." The data relative to this period is only the work-plan for this police, which means that the collective information or the collective plan for the work of reserve police stations, which means that each and every reserve police station should have submitted their report to the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you didn't understand my question. I'll just leave it as it is. Please, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to the next page in both languages and the paragraph right at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It states: "On the basis of the dispersion of traffic accidents in terms of place and time, the Prijedor police station will develop definite daily traffic control plans." And turning the page, the first full paragraph on the next page states: "In addition to traffic control and in co-operation with the Prijedor traffic safety police station, the Prijedor police station will monitor the work of vehicle inspection station, driving schools, and certain organisations." Again, these are references to the fact that the Prijedor police station was functioning at this time, May of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The employees functioned. The station didn't. This report was sent according to the peacetime plan and organisational work, because it was requested by the centre. I repeat: It stopped functioning on the 10th of September, 1991, and it didn't function up to the moment when the Dayton Accords were signed. Only the reserve police stations functioned. I keep on repeating that. There is physical evidence that proves it. The truth is I don't have that here; however, I showed the evidence to the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is ample piece of physical evidence that prove that the police station in Prijedor didn't function because people were assigned to the reserve police stations. One of the pieces of physical evidence were lists that were maintained daily and show that active duty officers had been assigned to the reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd appreciate if you could try to keep your answers focused on the specific question that I ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document. And I would like 65 ter 26043, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6676, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, this document is quite faint. However, I believe you have seen it before in your own trial. You're probably familiar with it. It is a decision of the Banja Luka CSB, dated 17 June, 1992. And it is assigning you to carry out the duties and tasks of commander of the Prijedor police station. And it is retroactive as of the 1st of April, 1992. Now, in this decision, Mr. Zupljanin is assigning you to carry out the duties and tasks of Prijedor police station commander, effective -- in the RS MUP, effect 1 April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I said that I was commander from 19 August and those were peacetime police stations that I commanded. This decision, dated 17 June, 1992, which was issued by the CSB, is a decision on the take -- taking me out from the organs of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and assigning me to work in the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina starting as of the 1st of April, 1992. I was temporarily assigned to the same job I previously held in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says here that the public security stations in the CSB would continue working as the organisational units of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in keeping with this law. And then there is a reference to me. Since on the 1st of April, 1992, I was still working in a body which had been abolished pursuant to Article 127 of the Law on Internal Affairs, he was engaged on the said date as an employee of the Banja Luka security services centre. So this is nothing else but a decision to transfer me from the non-existing Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the newly established Serbian MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina to occupy the same position that I had previously had. This is a very important decision because it ties over the period of my working in the previous institution to a different institution. It was important for my pension plan. It was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Transcript and possible --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation hasn't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you interrupted the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It means we didn't hear the last part of witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We missed after you said: "It was important for my pension plan ..." Did you have something further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pension plan and other benefits and my rights as an employee of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be clear if instead of the word "engaged" the word "retaken" were used. So he was not engaged. He was retaken from one institution that had been abolished, and he was reassigned to work in a newly established ministry. In order for that to become possible, a new decision had to be issued.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be heard on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you said there that, to the same effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that it was not just me who was reassigned. All the employees from the abolished organs and public security stations and CSBs who lived in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were reassigned to another new institution. I submitted a piece of physical evidence showing that I was issued with a document showing that my work engagement was abolished on the 1st of April, and it was only logical that from that time on we were taken on by the newly established Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me try this for the last time. So according to this document you were reassigned to Prijedor police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was taken over. I was the commander of that police station, but I was taken over. And as of the 1st of April, 1992, I continued working in a -- and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you not make your answer simpler. So according to this document, you were reassigned or retaken or reappointed as Prijedor police station, commander of Prijedor police station? That's what this document says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Taken over from the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic, which started operating at that time. And I had the same position as before. And the decision refers to the peacetime public security station in Prijedor. I was the peacetime commander all the time up to March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What about on the 17th of June, 1992? So is it your evidence in June 1992 this Prijedor police station did not operate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was abolished. However, it was still an organisational unit of the Ministry of the Interior in peacetime. It was an organisational unit of the public security station in peacetime, but it did not function. All that functioned were reserve police stations because people had been mobilised to reserve police stations because of the state of war. Peacetime organisation was suspended. It was abolished. It didn't exist at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we admit this document? Are you tendering this? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6677, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I could have 65 ter 25906, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jankovic, this is a Prijedor SJB document dated the 2nd of August, 1992, establishing a police battalion. It's signed by Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in English and at the bottom of the first page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It states the battalion command is composed as follows: Staff commander: Simo Drljaca, chief of the Prijedor SJB. And under number 3: Chief of staff: Dusan Jankovic, head of the police department. Earlier in your testimony, you denied being head of the uniformed police department. In this contemporaneous document, Simo Drljaca is identifying you as head of the police department, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me see. Based on the dispatches from the CSB Banja Luka, the public security station establishes a battalion made up of seven companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: And these companies are listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was very simple. In this contemporaneous document, Simo Drljaca is identifying you as head of the police department; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. But I want to explain why that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it up to the Chamber whether we should hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This battalion, these seven companies that Simo Drljaca set up in the area of Prijedor municipality, never actually operated in reality. This battalion was formed in the event they would need to go to the front line and place themselves at the disposal of the army. But the first mistake is that the commander of the battalion staff is Simo Drljaca; the deputy commander, Marko Djenadija; the Chief of Staff, Dusan Jankovic, who is chief of the police department. According to all the laws and military regulations and the regulations of internal affairs, in the battalion there is no chief of staff. The chief of staff exists only in a brigade that is made up of several battalions. Second, here where it says chief of or head of the police department, in order to have a head there should be a police department in Prijedor; however, not a single public security station in any municipality, not only in Prijedor, did not have a police department or a head of police department. Police departments existed only in CSBs. In order for a police department to exist at a level of a public security station - and in the staffing system it did not - there would have to be inspectors who go out and conduct inspections, et cetera. And we had no such people in the public security station of Prijedor. Mr. Drljaca, before becoming head of the -- or, rather, chief of the public security station, was some sort of senior executive in the education -- on the education board.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat and stop speaking so fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, interpreters couldn't follow you. But I would like Ms. Gustafson to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'll have you recognise Mr. Drljaca's signature, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then I would tender this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That is Mr. Drljaca's signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6678, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could with have 65 ter 26045, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jankovic, you can see this is a report conducted by police -- three police inspectors of the Prijedor SJB in February 1993. And the first part of the report listings the people who participated in the review of the Prijedor SJB's activities. And under number 3 it says: Dusan Jankovic, Chief, Prijedor, SJB, police department. And this is another contemporaneous reflection of your position as chief of the SJB police department, this time by three police inspectors; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is again a mistake. I was not a head of department. I was commander of the public security station in Prijedor, and Cadjo was not what it says here. He was commander of the reserve police station 1 and that's what he said before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in his testimony. There are several mistakes here. As I said, I was not head of the police department because in our staffing system, the public security station did not have a police department in any municipality. Not only Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6679, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jankovic, we've seen now five or six contemporaneous documents identifying you as police station commander or head of the police department of the SJB. I could go on, but I think the point has been made. But it is not just these documents that identify you in this manner. Your senior role in the SJB has also been confirmed by Prijedor SJB officials who have testified for the Defence; in particular, Miroslav Kvocka testified that when Fikret Kadiric was arrested in April or May 1992, you replaced him as commander of the Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that's D4219, paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And he identified you as second in command of the SJB after Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that was at paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And a protected witness, KW609, identified you as Simo Drljaca's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: D4246, paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So this is not just a technical administrative function that you had or coincidental series of mistakes in the documents. This is how police officials operating in Prijedor at the time understood your role, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Fikret Kadiric was not arrested when I became commander of the police station in Prijedor. Fikret Kadiric from the post of commander of the police station was reassigned to be commander in the traffic control station, and he remained there until the take-over. Witnesses can say here that I was deputy or this or that, but at the public security station there was no deputy or assistant chief. The assistant chief position only started from 1993 when the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was reorganised. I was assistant chief of the public security station and I was also assistant chief of the CSB, and I was also deputy chief of the public security station -- or, rather, CSB, and chief of public security in Prijedor. But all that was in 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998. In 1992, the position of chief of police department or head of police department or assistant chief of the public security station did not exist. I don't know what the witnesses here say, but I know that I did not have such a position in the time that you allege in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In November of last year, the Karadzic Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. The meaning is completely changed. The witness said: "I was in those positions but not in the alleged time."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, the Karadzic Defence on November 7th of last year filed a summary of your expected evidence, which says, among other things: "At the commencement of the war, he was the police chief in Prijedor." Now, are you aware that the party that is now putting you forward to say that you were not the chief of police at this time, and you worked in logistics, a few months ago actually expected you to testify that you were chief of police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear very well. Somebody turned down the volume. I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you start again?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Karadzic Defence in November of last year filed a summary of your expected evidence in this case. And it states, among other things: "At the commencement of the war, he was the police chief in Prijedor." Are you aware that the party that is now putting you forward to state that you were not the chief of police in Prijedor at this time - and, in fact, you just worked in logistics - a few months ago actually expected you to testify that you were the police chief in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Mr. Karadzic's Defence team and why they stated that. You'd better ask them. I can tell you that the head of the police department in public security stations in the time you allege did not exist as a position. Not before, not during the war, not later. The public police department or a head of police department did not exist at public security station level. That position existed only in security services centres such as in Banja Luka. That is my answer and that is the way it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I get an explanation. The reference that we asked the witness not to say -- or, rather, to say that he was not chief of police; line 17?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think that's a mischaracterisation of my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you -- the contemporaneous documents identify you as police station commander and/or chief of the police department. Your colleagues in SJB at the time identified you similarly. The Defence a few months ago identified you similarly. And that's what the judgement that convicted you found. And that's because that is, in fact, the role you had in the SJB at the time. This story about being involved in logistics is a fiction that you identified in order to attempt to minimise your culpability for the Koricanske Stijene massacre for which you were convicted and you're continuing that fiction in this courtroom; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not correct. I made a solemn declaration here to speak the truth. I wish to assist the Court to get at the truth in the case of Koricanske Stijene. And as for what you say, I've told you several times here and explained: I was commander of police station in peacetime, but nowhere in the world can you find one person who would be commander of police station and chief of police, et cetera. I was not chief, ever. I was assistant chief of the public security station. I was assistant chief of CSB and chief of CSB, et cetera, but not in that period in which you want to place me. I keep repeating that all the time. Take the rule book on staffing that prevailed at the time, and you will see that that position did not exist. As for what you assert, that I wish to deny a crime to which a court has linked me, that is not true either. I want to get at the truth because I have nothing to do with that crime. I wish I were the only one innocently, wrongly convicted, but I'm not and I'm interested in getting at the truth. The truth will out. It cannot be hidden forever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jankovic, earlier in your testimony you were asked about communication between the Prijedor SJB and the ministry, and you said that there were no dispatches between the Prijedor SJB and the republican MUP, but you also said at page 12 that the communication between Prijedor and the ministry went through the CSB. And that is correct, isn't it? The normal communication chain was from the Prijedor SJB to the Banja Luka CSB to the republican MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. I didn't say there was no communication between CSBs. I said there were communications and quite a few periods when that communication was broken down because there were power cuts and various things caused by the war in Prijedor. I know what I've said and I can repeat it any time you ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have P2744, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, this is the log-book of dispatches received by SJB Prijedor for 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to page 16 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see the first date refers to -- or states the 30th of April, 1992. And as you look down the page, you can see in -- through columns 2 and columns 8 that the Prijedor SJB is receiving numerous dispatches from CSB Banja Luka for the beginning of May. And if we could just -- if I could just have you look at the following two pages, pages 17 and 18, which show dispatches received throughout the month of May. And we can see they are all or virtually all from the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it shows the SJB receiving dispatches from the CSB Banja Luka on virtually a daily basis throughout May of 1992. And I can tell you that the log-book continues this way throughout 1992, with virtually daily communications from the CSB. In your testimony you said that there was only communication between the SJB and CSB when there was electricity. Now, do you accept that this document shows that, in fact, the SJB was able to receive communications from the CSB on basically a daily basis in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There were times when there was no electricity, but they probably turned on the power generator when they needed to receive a dispatch. I don't see that this is communication on a daily basis. 28th May, for instance, is one entry, and then 2nd of June, then 4th of June. There were times when they could receive and times when they couldn't receive. I can't tell you when they could and when they couldn't. This document probably reflects the real situation with dispatch communications between the SJB Prijedor and the CSB Banja Luka. And this was handled by the communication centre at the SJB. They received and sent out dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier today you were asked about Keraterm and whether you heard of any unusual event at Keraterm, and you testified that you heard there was a mutiny on the part of the detainees there. And in that process, the mutineers were killed. Now, you heard about this killing of Keraterm detainees the very same day it happened; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Everybody in Prijedor heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. Everyone in Prijedor heard about that. And the Prijedor police did not carry out any formal investigation into this killing, did it, at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they did or didn't, but it was a serious crime so the CSB Banja Luka and the higher court in Banja Luka had jurisdiction. The lower court in Banja Luka dealt with less serious crimes that fell within its purview, whereas the CSB was in charge of crimes that fell under the jurisdiction of the higher court, and they helped conduct on-site investigation within their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said you didn't know whether an investigation was carried out or not. The evidence the Trial Chamber has received about this incident is that this was a huge massacre of prisoners in their cells in cold blood. The army came in, set up a machine-gun on a table outside one of the detention rooms, lit it with a floodlight, and massacred roughly 150 detainees. Now, if there had been a proper investigation reflecting the scale and severity of this crime at the time, you would have heard about it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If it's about the army, if the army was involved, then the on-site investigation would be done by military organs. If not, if this was not done by the civilian authorities, it was done by the army, and military organs had the jurisdiction in all matters concerning the army. We had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, as you know, because you testified this detention facility was secured by police officers, so it was -- obviously involved both army and police. But in any event, Mr. Jankovic, if this extremely serious crime had actually been properly investigated at the time, you would have heard about it, no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly an investigation was carried out without me hearing about it. It's possible. I just don't know and I can't say anything about things I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about Koricanske Stijene now. You explained in your testimony that the day after the massacre, the 22nd of August, you and Mr. Cadjo were summoned by the chief of the public security department of the CSB Banja Luka, Djuro Bulic, to Banja Luka and questioned about what had happened the previous day. Now, first of all, you agree that if you were in fact just a police officer carrying out logistic tasks, as you claim, it wouldn't make any sense for Mr. Bulic to summon you along with Mr. Cadjo to Banja Luka to answer questions about this crime, would it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have also said before the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina that I never quite understood why he summoned me. But probably Djuro Bulic was chief of sector of public security at the level of the CSB Banja Luka. As far as I understood, when we were summoned it was not about any questioning. He just informed us of the newly arisen situation in connection with a crime that had been committed, and he probably thought that he would find out more about the crime, who ordered it, who organised it, who executed it. But Simo Drljaca came to that meeting and so he threw out me and Cadjo. And the chief told him, anyway, that he should not have summoned us without his knowledge, that he should only have summoned us if the chief -- through the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And later that day, the 22nd of August, you returned to the Prijedor SJB. And again, you saw Simo Drljaca there who was visibly annoyed and upset because both Mr. Zupljanin and Mico Stanisic had been informed about the crime and the perpetrators; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Simo Drljaca when I returned to the SJB. When we were returning from the CSB on the way from Banja Luka to Prijedor, Cadjo, the commander of the reserve police station, Prijedor centre, called the duty service, of whom he was commander, and told them to wait for him in his office. When we arrived at the SJB we went to his office and we found there five assistant commanders. If you want me to, I can give you the names of those people. Do you need the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Cadjo informed them that we had been summoned to Banja Luka, he told them what had happened in Banja Luka, and these men said they had been informed already because they had read the dispatch from Colonel Peulic, commander of the 22nd Brigade, which brigade in the meantime had arrived in Prijedor, and then we sat down to agree how to act in that situation because all of us at that meeting were professional policemen. And some conclusions were agreed upon, and the chief of the SJB -- sorry, chief of the CSB Banja Luka was informed of these conclusions. After the meeting we continued sitting and talking when Simo Drljaca arrived, obviously upset, and he said he had informed CSB Banja Luka and Chief Zupljanin about who had escorted the convoy and who the possible perpetrators of the crime were. And then you know the rest, how it went on, how the investigation or inquiry was conducted, et cetera. That crime was not something that anybody wanted to cover up, if that's what you are insinuating. On the same date, 22nd August, everybody already knew who escorted the convoy and how the thing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When I first asked you about Simo Drljaca at the Prijedor SJB on the 22nd of August after you returned from Banja Luka, you said: "I didn't see Simo Drljaca when I returned to the SJB." But your answer makes clear that you did actually see him that day, visibly annoyed and upset, at the Prijedor SJB, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what you said. You said when we came to the SJB, we saw Simo Drljaca. We came to the SJB, had a meeting there where we adopted certain conclusions, and it was only later on that Simo Drljaca joined us from Banja Luka and came to the conference room where we had our meeting. That's why I said what I said, because Simo Drljaca wasn't there in the SJB as we got there. He only joined us later after having come from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 26028, please. Page 20 of the English, page 19 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, earlier today you testified that after this massacre there were proposals that those who escorted the convoy be arrested and prosecuted but that the platoon escaped to Kozara. And then they resisted arrest and then there were negotiations with the SJB chief. I'd like to direct your attention to your previous testimony in your own trial on this point, which is towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and right near the middle in the English. And you're asked: "Tell us about the behaviour of the convoy escorts immediately after the crime was committed?" And you said: "The entire intervention platoon beat a hasty retreat to Mount Kozara. Not only those who took part in the convoy escort but the entire intervention platoon." You said: "Later on they returned and cleared up the terrain, and after that they went to Han Pijesak, theater of operations, as a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska." Now, that reference to the platoon returning to clear up the terrain refers to the fact that the intervention platoon was ordered to go back to the massacre site to clear up the bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Today I said that the entire intervention platoon went to Mount Kozara as renegades. I didn't say anything else. Before the negotiations in which Commander Paras and the SJB in Prijedor were involved in, I don't know how the negotiations ran and what was their course. I only know that following these negotiations, they went out on the ground to clear up the terrain and that is all I know of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Clear up the terrain at the execution site; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you would agree as a career police professional that no proper investigation would involve sending the alleged perpetrators back to the crime scene to clean it up, would you it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who sent them there or what their assignment up there was. This is something that the person who sent them up there and who was there would know. I didn't attend the meetings either in Prijedor or in Banja Luka which dealt with this problem, so I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, it's -- you testified that it was impossible to arrest this unit. It is your position, then, that this unit obeyed an order to go back to the execution site to clear up the bodies, yet it was impossible to detain these 40 men. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. You want me to answer this. I said that it was impossible to arrest them. Perhaps this was the result of an agreement between Commander Paras and the chief of the SJB. I don't know what compromise or agreement was reached, what was agreed. This is unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The evidence in this case in the form of Simo Drljaca's annual report states that at this time the manpower of the Prijedor SJB was over 1500 men. Again, Mr. Jankovic, is it your position that 1500 men were unable to arrest the 40 intervention platoon members?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Those 1500 men were assigned to the reserve police stations, including the active police force. The only organisation which could have intervened and was prepared and ready for combat was the intervention platoon. They were people who were ready for combat. The rest were patrolling police officers, duty police officers. It would have been completely senseless to send these people there because it would have resulted in bloodshed. This was the only way to see the matter through to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
